parts.latex:
A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound.

A scientist wants to explore the relationship between the temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval.

Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below.

\begin{itemize}
\item A box-plot of the temperature data is shown.

\exfigure{34_q27_1}
\item The mean temperature in the dataset is $0.525^\circ\text{C}$ below the median temperature in the dataset.
\item A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points.
\end{itemize}

The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data $(x,y)$, where $x$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $y$ is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is

$$y=-10.6063+bx,$$

where $b$ is the slope of the regression line.

The least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the temperature data and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the chirp data.

Calculate the number of chirps expected in a 15-second interval when the temperature is $19^\circ$ Celsius. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
parts.note: Least-squares regression with box-plot data: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= 22 - 0.525 \\ &= 21.475 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{y} &= \dfrac{684}{20} \\ &= 34.2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ into the regression equation, we have
$$\begin{aligned} 34.2 &= -10.6063 + b(21.475) \\ \dfrac{44.8063}{21.475} &= b \\ b &= 2.08644\ldots \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 19$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -10.6063 + 2.08644\ldots \times 19 \\ &= 29.03606\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 29 chirps are expected.

The point $T$ is the peak of a mountain and the point $O$ is directly below the mountain's peak. The point $Y$ is due east of $O$ and the angle of elevation of $T$ from $Y$ is $60^\circ$. The point $F$ is 4 km south-west of $Y$. The points $O$, $Y$ and $F$ are on level ground. The angle of elevation of $T$ from $F$ is $45^\circ$.

\exfigure{1630_q29_1}

parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle TYO$, right-angled at $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{OY} \\ \therefore\ OY &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
The exact value $\tan 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}$ comes from the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle:

\exfigure{1630_q29_s1}

In $\triangle TFO$, $\angle TFO=45^\circ$, $\angle TOF=90^\circ$

$\therefore\ \angle OTF=45^\circ$

$\therefore\ \triangle TFO$ is isosceles and $OF=h$

In $\triangle FOY$, $\angle OYF=45^\circ$ ($F$ is south-west of $Y$ and $O$ is due west of $Y$). By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 &= \left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+4^2-2\times 4\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 45^\circ \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+16-\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{2h^2}{3}+\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}}-16=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{-\frac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\pm\sqrt{\frac{64}{6}+4\times\frac{2}{3}\times 16}}{\frac{4}{3}} \\ &= 3.03 \quad\text{since } h>0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds a quadratic expression in $h$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to use the cosine rule to find a value for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1630_q29_s2}

In $\triangle FOY$, let $\theta=\angle OFY$. By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}} &= \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{h} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3}} \\ \theta &= 24.09\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 24^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$Y$ is on a bearing of $045^\circ$ from $F$, and $O$ is $\theta$ further anticlockwise:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 45^\circ-24^\circ \\ &\approx 021^\circ \end{aligned}$$

Contributions are every 6 months for 5 years, so $n=5\times2=10$ periods, at $r=\dfrac{2\%}{2}=1\%=0.01$ per period.

Doubling a contribution adds another $\$750$, so if the last $m$ contributions are doubled, the extra amount is $\$750$ times the future value of an annuity of $\$1$ for $m$ periods, $\text{FV}_m$. We need
$$\begin{aligned} 7846.65+750\times\text{FV}_m&\ge14\,000\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge\dfrac{14\,000-7846.65}{750}\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge8.2045\end{aligned}$$
From the table, $\text{FV}_8=8.2857\ge8.2045$, while $\text{FV}_7=\dfrac{1.01^7-1}{0.01}\approx7.2135<8.2045$.

So at least the last $8$ contributions must be doubled, leaving at most $10-8=2$ contributions of $\$750$.

Check: $750\times10.4622+750\times8.2857=\$14\,060.93\ge\$14\,000$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum number of } \$750 \text{ contributions}=2$$

A pyramid $MABCD$ has its vertex $M$ vertically above $O$, the centre of its square base $ABCD$, as shown. $AM=\ell$ cm and makes an angle of $\theta$ with the base.

\exfigure{1632_q30_1}

parts.latex:

Show that $V=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $\theta$, in radians, for which the volume of the pyramid is a maximum. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

solutions.latex:
In triangle $AOM$ (right angle at $O$, $\angle MAO=\theta$), using the sine and cosine ratios:
$$\begin{aligned} MO&=\ell\sin\theta\\ AO&=\ell\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is the centre of the square, so the diagonal $AC=2AO=2\ell\cos\theta$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, a square with side $s$ has $s^2+s^2=AC^2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{base area}=s^2&=\dfrac{(2\ell\cos\theta)^2}{2}\\ &=2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
The volume of a pyramid is $\dfrac{1}{3}\times\text{base area}\times\text{height}$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\times\ell\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the base area $2\ell^2\cos^2\theta$ and the height $\ell\sin\theta$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Checked with l=1, theta=pi/4: half-diagonal 0.7071, side 1, height 0.7071, V=0.2357 = (2/3)(0.7071)(0.5).

solutions.latex:
Here $\ell$ is constant and $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=\cos^2\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-2\cos\theta\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{d\theta}&=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\left(\cos^3\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta\left(\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta\right)\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $\cos\theta\ne0$ when $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta&=0\\ \tan^2\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} &&(\tan\theta>0)\\ \theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\approx0.6155\end{aligned}$$
Nature: $\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta>0$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ is decided by
$$\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\left(1-2\tan^2\theta\right)$$
that is, by $1-2\tan^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=0.5: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx0.40>0 &&V \text{ increasing}\\ \theta&=0.7: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx-0.42<0 &&V \text{ decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the stationary point is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \theta\approx0.62$$
criteria: Finds $\theta\approx0.62$ without justifying the maximum, or equivalent merit
Finds a correct factorised $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ and sets it equal to $0$, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ using the product rule, or equivalent merit

parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $TCA$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 35^\circ=\dfrac{40}{AC}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ AC &= \dfrac{40}{\tan 35^\circ}\\ &= 57.1259\ldots\\ &= 57.13 \text{ metres} \quad (\text{2 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

In right-angled triangle $TCB$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{40}{BC}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ BC &= \dfrac{40}{\tan 30^\circ}\\ &= 69.28 \text{ metres} \quad (\text{2 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ACB$, with $AC=57.13$ from part (a) and $AB=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle ACB &= \dfrac{57.13^2+69.28^2-100^2}{2\times(57.13)\times(69.28)}\\ &= -0.24462\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle ACB=104^\circ \quad (\text{nearest degree})$$
$A$ is due east of $C$ (bearing $090^\circ$), so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } B \text{ from } C &= 104^\circ+90^\circ\\ &= 194^\circ\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A vertical tower of height $h$ metres stands on horizontal ground. From a point $P$ on the ground due east of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $45^\circ$. From a point $Q$ on the ground due south of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $30^\circ$. If the distance $PQ$ is 40 metres, find the exact height of the tower.

\exfigure{1359_q29_1}
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
Let $R$ be the base of the tower. In right-angled triangles $PRT$ and $QRT$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \qquad \tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ PR &= h & QR &= \sqrt{3}h \end{aligned}$$
$P$ is due east and $Q$ due south of $R$, so $\angle PRQ = 90^\circ$. Using Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle PRQ$:
$$\begin{aligned} 40^2 &= h^2 + \left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2 \\ 1600 &= 4h^2 \\ h^2 &= 400 \\ h &= \pm 20 \end{aligned}$$
$h > 0$, so $h = 20$ m.

At 9 a.m., two destroyers start travelling from $A$ and $B$ in the direction of $C$ and continue past $C$ in the same straight lines. The destroyer at $A$ travels along $AC$ with a uniform speed of $20$ km/h, while the destroyer at $B$ travels along $BC$ with a uniform speed of $50$ km/h.

parts.latex:
The destroyers are known to be “on alert” when they are less than $40$ km apart.

During what times will the two destroyers be “on alert”?
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

solutions.latex:
Using the bearings from $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ACB&=250^{\circ}-130^{\circ}\\ &=120^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$
Let $AC=x$. In right-angled triangle $AHC$, the angle of depression gives $\angle HAC=60^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^{\circ}&=\dfrac{h}{x}\\ x&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^{\circ}}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\\ h&=\sqrt{3}x \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $BHC$, $\angle HBC=30^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 30^{\circ}&=\dfrac{h}{BC}\\ BC&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 30^{\circ}}=\dfrac{h}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}=\sqrt{3}h\\ &=\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}x=3x \end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$, $AB^2=AC^2+BC^2-2\times AC\times BC\times\cos 120^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(100\sqrt{13}\right)^2&=\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2-2\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ 10\,000\times 13&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2+h^2\\ 130\,000&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+4h^2=\dfrac{13h^2}{3}\\ 13h^2&=3\times 130\,000\\ h^2&=3\times 10\,000\\ h&=\pm\sqrt{30\,000} \end{aligned}$$
$h>0$, so $h=\sqrt{30\,000}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ AC=x&=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{30\,000}}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{10\,000}=100\text{ km}\\ BC&=\sqrt{3}h=\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{30\,000}=\sqrt{90\,000}=300\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
Or, using $BC=3x$:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2&=x^2+(3x)^2-2\times x\times 3x\times\cos 120^{\circ}\\ \left(100\sqrt{13}\right)^2&=x^2+9x^2-6x^2\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ 10\,000\times 13&=10x^2+3x^2\\ 130\,000&=13x^2\\ x^2&=10\,000 \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$, so $x=100$, and $BC=3x=300$ km.
criteria: Uses the cosine rule correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds $AC$ and $BC$ in terms of $h$ (or $BC=3x$), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours the distances $AC$ and $BC$ are $100-20t$ and $300-50t$ respectively. The angle at $C$ is still $120^{\circ}$, so by the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2&=(100-20t)^2+(300-50t)^2-2(100-20t)(300-50t)\cos 120^{\circ}\\ &=10\,000-4000t+400t^2+90\,000-30\,000t+2500t^2-2\left(30\,000-5000t-6000t+1000t^2\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=130\,000-45\,000t+3900t^2\\ &=100\left(1300-450t+39t^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
$AB>0$, so
$$\begin{aligned} AB&=\sqrt{100\left(1300-450t+39t^2\right)}\\ &=10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes the correct distances after $t$ hours into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

The destroyers are on alert when $AB<40$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}&<40\\ \sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}&<4 &&(\text{divide by } 10)\\ 1300-450t+39t^2&<16 &&(\text{square})\\ 39t^2-450t+1284&<0 &&(\text{subtract } 16) \end{aligned}$$
Solving $39t^2-450t+1284=0$ with the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{450\pm\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{2\times 39}\\ &=\dfrac{450\pm\sqrt{2196}}{78}\\ &=\dfrac{75\pm\sqrt{61}}{13} \end{aligned}$$

$$5\text{ h }10\text{ min }6.39\text{ s}<t<6\text{ h }22\text{ min }12.07\text{ s}$$
where $t$ is the time after 9 am.

In right-angled triangle $AOT$:

$$\angle AOB=270^\circ-240^\circ=30^\circ$$
Applying the cosine rule in triangle $AOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}10^2&=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2+(OB)^2-2\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(OB)\cos 30^\circ\\ 100&=\dfrac{27}{4}+(OB)^2-3\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(OB)\\ (OB)^2-\dfrac{9}{2}(OB)-\dfrac{373}{4}&=0\\ 4(OB)^2-18(OB)-373&=0\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}OB&=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{18^2-4\times 4\times(-373)}}{2\times 4}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{6292}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm 22\sqrt{13}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pm 11\sqrt{13}}{4}\end{aligned}$$

$$OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\text{ metres}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{4x-\tan 2x}{\sin 5x}$

David is in a life raft, $D$, and Anna is in a cabin cruiser, $A$, searching for him.

They are in contact by mobile telephone. David tells Anna that he can see the top of the mountain Mt Hope, $H$.

From David's position, the mountain has a bearing of $340^\circ$ and the angle of elevation to the top of the mountain is $12^\circ$.

Anna can also see Mt Hope. From her position, the mountain has a bearing of $070^\circ$ and the top of the mountain has an angle of elevation of $19^\circ$. The top of Mt Hope is $1\,244$ m above sea level.

\exfigure{339_q33_1}

Find the distance of the life raft from Anna's position.

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{339_q33_s1}

Let $B$ be the point at sea level directly below $H$, so $HB=1244$ m.

In $\triangle ABH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle AHB=90^\circ-19^\circ=71^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s2}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 71^\circ &= \dfrac{AB}{1244} \\ AB &= 1244\tan 71^\circ \end{aligned}$$

In $\triangle BDH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle BHD=90^\circ-12^\circ=78^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s3}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 78^\circ &= \dfrac{BD}{1244} \\ BD &= 1244\tan 78^\circ \end{aligned}$$

The bearings of $B$ from $A$ ($070^\circ$) and from $D$ ($340^\circ$) differ by $70^\circ+20^\circ=90^\circ$, so $\angle ABD=90^\circ$.

By Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle ABD$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD^2 &= AB^2+BD^2 \\ &= (1244\tan 71^\circ)^2+(1244\tan 78^\circ)^2 \\ &= 47\,305\,057.68 \end{aligned}$$

Since $AD>0$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD &= \sqrt{47\,305\,057.68} \\ &= 6877.867\ldots \\ &\approx 6877.87\text{ m (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$

parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle with the angle of elevation $30^\circ$ at $D$ and height $h$ at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{AD}\\AD&=\dfrac{h}{\sin30^\circ}=2h\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is $10$ m above $A$ and $OB$ is horizontal, so $B$ is $h+10$ m above the ground:
$$BD=\dfrac{h+10}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: One correct expression, $AD=2h$ or $BD=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OAB$, $OA=OB=10$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$, so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$AB=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt{2}$$
In $\triangle ABD$, use the cosine rule with $\angle ADB=30^\circ$:
$$\left(10\sqrt{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+(2h)^2-2\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)(2h)\cos30^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}200&=\dfrac{4h^2+80h+400}{3}+4h^2-4h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2+80h+400+12h^2-12h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2-40h+400\\0&=4h^2-40h-200\\&=4\left(h^2-10h-50\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$h=\dfrac{10\pm\sqrt{300}}{2}=5\pm5\sqrt{3}$$
Since $h>0$:
$$\therefore\ h=5+5\sqrt{3}\approx13.66$$
criteria: Correct quadratic equation in $h$, or equivalent merit
$AB=10\sqrt{2}$ and correct cosine rule equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Two identical right pyramids with square bases and equilateral triangular faces are joined to form a regular octahedron.

The following diagram shows a regular octahedron with edge length 6 cm and centre at $O$. $AM$ and $ME$ are perpendicular heights of $\Delta ABC$ and $\Delta BCE$ respectively and point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

\exfigure{382_q21_1}

Find the size of $\angle AME$, to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
By symmetry $\triangle AMO\cong\triangle EMO$ (SSS: $AM=EM$, $AO=EO$, $MO$ common), so
$$\angle AME=2\times\angle AMO$$
In $\triangle AMC$ ($\angle AMC=90^\circ$, $AC=6$, $MC=3$), by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} AM &= \sqrt{6^2-3^2} \\ &= \sqrt{27} \\ &= 3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle AMO$ (right angle at $O$, with $MO=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6=3$, half the side of the square base):
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle AMO &= \dfrac{MO}{AM} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \angle AMO &= \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle AME &= 2\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\ &= 109.4712\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 109^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Accept an alternative using the sine rule (finding $AM$ and $AE$, then the angle).
